g.text: Within the Windows security ecosystem, there are the two main variables of the object security equation.
• Tokens : they identify the security context of a process or a thread,
• Security descriptors : they contain the security information associated with an object.
to achieve the CIA triad, many OSs use ACLs, which are describes as (according to RFC4949) :
"a mechanism that implements access control for a system resource by enumerating the system entities that are permitted to access the resource and
stating, either implicitly or explicitly, the access modes granted to each entity"
Access control policies dictate what types of access are permitted, under what circumstances, and by whom. there are 4 types :
• Discretionary access control (DAC) --> controls access based on the requestor's identity and access rules stating what requestors are (or are not)
allowed to do. An entity having access to a resource may enable another entity to access same resource
• Mandatory access control (MAC) --> an entity having access to a resource may NOT enable another entity to access same resource
• Role-based access control (RBAC) --> often seen in web apps, access is given according to role (admin, moderator, simple user... etc)
• Attribute-based access control (ABAC) --> evaluates attributes (or characteristics), rather than roles, to determine access
• The image shows the DACL/ACL for the user account "forend"
• Each item under "Permission entries" makes up the DACL for the user account.
• The individual entries (such as Full Control or Change Password) are Access
Control Entries (ACEs) showing the access rights granted over this user object to
In Windows, every object (also known as securable objects) has a security descriptor data structure that
specifies who can perform what actions on the object. The security descriptor is a binary data structure that,
although it can vary in length and exact contents, can contain six main fields:
• Revision Number: The SRM (Security Reference Monitor) version of the security model used to create the
• Control Flags: Optional modifiers that define the behavior/characteristics of the security descriptor.
• Owner SID: The object's owner SID.
• Group SID: The object's primary group SID. Only the Windows POSIX subsystem utilized this member (before
being discontinued), and most AD environments now ignore it.
• Discretionary access control list (DACL): Specifies who has what access to the object
• System access control list (SACL): Specifies which operations by which users should be logged in the security
audit log and the explicit integrity level of an object.
Internally, Windows represents a security descriptor via the SECURITY_DESCRIPTOR struct:
absolute security descriptors contain pointers to the information (i.e.,
not the actual information itself), as in the SECURITY_DESCRIPTOR
struct above, and these are the ones that we will encounter when
interacting with Windows objects, whether AD ones or not.
Self-relative security descriptors are not very different: instead of
storing pointers, they store the actual data of a security
descriptor in a contiguous memory block. These are meant to store a
security descriptor on a disk or transmit it over the wire.
A security descriptor can be one of two forms,
for the exploitation of DACLs, four of the seven members of the SECURITY_DESCRIPTOR struct are interesting for us :
The Control member is of type SECURITY_DESCRIPTOR_CONTROL, a 16-bit set of bit flags that qualify the
meaning of a security descriptor or its components. The value of Control, when retrieved with the function
GetSecurityDescriptorControl, can include a combination of 13 bits flags as shown in the image
These binary flags can be added to represent any combinations.
One important flag for us to know about is SE_DACL_PRESENT:
The "Owner" and "Group" members contain a pointer to the Security Identifier (SID) of the object's owner and primary group, respectively. Object owners are always
granted full control of the security descriptor, as they are granted the access rights RIGHT_WRITE_DAC (WriteDacl) and RIGHT_READ_CONTROL
In Windows, SACL (System access control list) and DACL (Discretionary access control lists) are the two types of access control lists
A SACL consists of a header and zero or more ACEs that dictate the types of access attempts that generate audit records in the
security event log of a domain controller;
SACL allows administrators to log access attempts to securable objects. There are two types of ACEs within a SACL,
DACL consists of a header and zero or more ACEs that dictate what principals have control rights over a specific object.
the struct definition of an ACL (from the kernel's point of view) can be observed in the image --->
An ACE contains a set of user rights and a SID that identifies a principal for whom the rights are allowed, denied,
Windows represents an ACE internally via the struct ACE_HEADER:
In a DACL, there can be nine types of ACEs :
-> the struct ACE_HEADER as a member,
-> the Mask member (which is of type ACCESS_MASK and defines the standard, specific, and generic rights)
-> SidStart (which holds the first 32 bits of the trustee's SID):
example of an ACE type showcasing the three common components
Four main types of ACEs are important for us to understand:
ACEs that include the keyword "Object" are object-specific ACEs used only within Active Directory. In addition to the
members of generic ACEs structure, object-specific ACEs contain the members:
• ObjectType: A GUID containing a type of child object, a property set or property, an extended right, or a validated write.
• InheritedObjectType: Specifies the type of child object that can inherit the ACE.
• Flags: Indicates whether the members ObjectType and InheritedObjectType are present via a set of bit flags.

BloodHound gathers all DACLs and correlates them to allow the analysis of rights in graph models, making finding abusable access rights easy.
BloodHound makes auditing easier by separating control rights into two categories:
• Inbound Control Rights: This is similar to inspecting an object's DACL.
• Outbound Control Rights: An aggregation and correlation of all references to
the object's SID in all DACLs across the domain.

When a client requests a Kerberos TGS service ticket, it gets encrypted with the service account’s NTLM password hash.
An attacker can obtain this ticket and perform offline password cracking to open it. If successful, the attacker can obtain the service account’s password.

Microsoft's Local Administrator Password Solution (LAPS) allows companies to manage the local Administrator password (randomized, unique, and changed regularly)
on domain-joined computers. These passwords are centrally stored in Active Directory and restricted to authorized users using ACLs.
Passwords are protected in transit from the client to the server using Kerberos v5 and AES. Here is how it works:
-> A LAPS client is installed on each computer. This client is responsible for periodically changing the local administrator password on the computer.
-> The password is stored in Active Directory as an attribute of the computer object. This attribute is named ms-MCS-AdmPwd.
-> To access the local administrator password for a computer, we can use the LAPS UI tool or PowerShell to retrieve the current password from Active Directory.
-> The password is only visible to users granted permission to read it.
This is possible when the controlled account has one of the following over the target:
--> ReadProperty access right over the attribute ms-MCS-AdmPwd and if ms-MCS-AdmPwdExpirationTime is set

Group Managed Service Accounts (gMSAs) is a feature in Microsoft Active Directory that provides a secure and automated mechanism for managing service
accounts used by applications and services running on Windows servers.
gMSAs have built-in password management and simplified key distribution.
When a gMSA is created, it is associated with a specific Active Directory group, allowing multiple servers or applications to share the same gMSA for
A gMSA leverages a secure key distribution process, where the password is automatically generated, securely stored, and periodically rotated by the Active
By utilizing gMSAs, the associated principals (such as machine accounts, servers, or applications) are granted specific access rights through the use of a
dedicated DACLs stored in the msDS-GroupMSAMembership attribute of the service account.
These access rights can be tailored to meet the specific requirements of each principal, granting them access to the necessary resources.

PKINIT is a pre-authentication extension that extends the Kerberos Protocol to use public key cryptography and ticket-granting ticket (TGT) data signing

For compatibility purposes, when a client uses PKINIT and needs to communicate with a service that doesn't support Kerberos authentication, NTLM is used.
Microsoft introduced a special Service Ticket as an alternative authentication method to address that, this special TGS contains the NTLM hash inside the
Privilege Attribute Certificate (PAC) in an encrypted NTLM_SUPPLEMENTAL_CREDENTIAL entity.
The encrypted PAC is stored within the ticket, which is encrypted using the key of the service it was issued for. For a TGT, the ticket is encrypted using the
key of the KRBTGT account, which the client cannot decrypt. To obtain a ticket that can be decrypted, the client needs to perform Kerberos User-to-User
Every time a client requests a TGT, a new session key is created. The KDC does not keep a record of active session keys but extracts the session key from
the client's ticket. When a user requests a U2U TGS-REQ, the KDC uses the target user's TGT as an additional ticket in the response. The KDC then
extracts the session key from the encrypted part of the TGT and generates a new service ticket.
The above means that if we request a U2U Service Ticket from ourselves to ourselves, we will be able to decrypt the ticket and access the PAC and the NTLM
hash because the key used to encrypt the ticket is in our possession. By modifying the msDS-KeyCredentialLink property, we can also obtain a user's or

System administrators use "logon scripts" to automate various user tasks or configurations when logging into the domain, such as mapping and
unmapping network drives, auditing and reporting, gathering information, and environment customization.
There are two methods for assigning users a logon script:
1- By using the Logon script field in the Profile tab of the user properties dialog, which internally updates the scriptPath attribute
The scriptPath attribute (part of the User-Logon property set) specifies the path
for a user's logon script; when setting it via the Logon script field in the Profile
tab of a user's properties dialog in ADUC, AD updates scriptPath accordingly:
• programs written in any language hosted by the "Windows Script Host
• KiXtart, a logon script processor and enhanced batch scripting language.
however, we can run PowerShell commands from within batch and VBScript files.
To allow for replication to all domain controllers in the domain, Windows stores logon
scripts in the scripts folder within the SYSVOL network share (which, on a domain
controller, resides at the physical location %systemroot%\SYSVOL\sysvol);
--> SYSVOL also stores domain and system policies, including Group Policy Objects.
The NETLOGON network share holds all the logon scripts that reside in the
The LOGONSERVER environment variable (evaluates to the NetBIOS name of the
domain controller that authenticated the current user) can help us locate the
For Windows to be able to execute them once a user logs into the domain, Logon
scripts set via the scriptPath attribute (which are known as Legacy logon scripts)
must be placed within the NETLOGON share; it is not possible to have them on a
different network share, regardless whether they are local or remote ones.
Alternatively, a logon script that applies to all domain users can be set in Group
Policy (which are known as Modern logon scripts) using the setting found at User
In addition to all the languages that scriptPath supports, this Group Policy setting
supports using PowerShell scripts for logon scripts:

(both NTFS permissions and share permissions), we can set a user's
scriptPath to a custom exploit script.
We can inspect the permissions we have on the file scriptPath points to
If write permissions on that script file, we can execute the same attacks as
if we had write rights on scriptPath without requiring write permissions
anywhere within NETLOGON; this becomes particularly valuable when a "stub"
logon script is employed, where scriptPath points to another file containing
the actual logon script code, often stored in a network share other than
NETLOGON (which domain users might have write permissions on).

SPN Jacking is an alternative method to abuse WriteSPN rights. It mixes DACL Abuse with manipulating Constrained Delegation to allow the abuse of
WriteSPN when password cracking is not possible.
Let's refresh on how Constrained Delegation works. We showcase a scenario where we compromise the WEBSRV server with constrained delegation
we can compromise DBSRV by authenticating to the SQL
service or by changing the service to an alternative, such as
CIFS. However, we can't compromise the other servers shown
in the image (FILESRV or EXCHSRV) because WEBSRV doesn't
have those servers listed in its SPN. This is where SPN
SPN jacking works by using WriteSPN rights to remove the
SQL/DBSRV SPN from DBSRV and assigns it to a target
machine. For example, if we want to compromise FILESRV and
have WriteSPN or similar permissions over it, we can register
the SPN SQL/DBSRV to FILESRV. Once this is done, any
TGS request for SQL/DBSRV will be encrypted for FILESRV,
allowing us to impersonate any user on that machine.
In this session, we will explore various techniques for abusing
SPN jacking, along with the conditions required for the attack

The NoPAC attack, commonly associated with the vulnerabilities CVE-2021-42278 and CVE-2021-42287, refers to a method where a Domain User can
perform privilege escalation and impersonate any privilege account through what is known as sAMAccountName Spoofing.
The attack starts with CVE-2021-42278, which exploits the lack of restrictions on modifications to the sAMAccountName attribute in Active Directory.
By default, Windows Active Directory does not enforce strict validation of this attribute, particularly ensuring that computer account names end with a
$ sign to distinguish them from user accounts. When we have sufficient permissions on a machine account, we can change the sAMAccountName of that
account to the name of a domain controller without the $. This modification sets up the scenario for impersonating a domain controller.
After changing the sAMAccountName to a domain controller's name (without the trailing $), we can exploit CVE-2021-42287. This vulnerability lies within
the Key Distribution Center. The KDC is tricked during the Service Ticket request phase. When a Service Ticket is requested for a non-existent account,
the KDC will append a $ and search again.
The exploitation process makes use of this behavior. We request a Ticket Granting Ticket (TGT) using the modified sAMAccountName, and then request
a Service Ticket, the KDC fails to find the account and appends a $ sign, unintentionally matching the legitimate domain controller's account, and finally
we get a Service Ticket with the domain controller's privileges.
----> An attacker with control over a machine or user account renames its sAMAccountName to a DC name without $, obtains a TGT, then reverts the
name and abuses KDC fallback to append $ during S4U—yielding a DC-privileged service ticket. Ticket PAC behavior and the domain’s

Centralized management of Windows settings for users/computers in an Active
Directory (AD) environment, applied via Group Policy Management Console
• GPC (Group Policy Container): LDAP object, stores metadata & permissions.
• GPT (Group Policy Template): Files in SYSVOL containing actual settings.
GPOs are linked to Sites, Domains, or Organizational Units (OUs).
OUs allow targeted policies for specific groups (e.g., HR, IT, POS systems).
To link GPOs: Modify Permissions on Site/Domain/OU.
Edit settings, delete, and modify security — full control over GPO.
Creating a GPO does nothing until linked to a Site/Domain/OU.
OU-level link → applies to specific departments/regions.
GPOs apply in this order (later overrides earlier unless enforced):
Multiple GPOs per level: processed by Link Order (lower number = later
Enforced GPO: overrides lower-level settings even if inheritance is blocked.
Block Inheritance: prevents higher-level GPOs from applying unless enforced.
Attacker with GPO modification or linking rights can push malicious
Modify GPO → allows editing policies to run code/actions on all linked computers.
Link GPO → can attach a GPO to Sites/Domains/OUs (needs Modify/Create rights to be useful).
Create GPO + Link GPO → full control over target scope.
---> GPOs apply only when linked to Sites/Domains/OUs.
gplink shows links + options: 0 = enabled, 1 = disabled, 2 = enforced, 3 = enforced+disabled.
look for SIDs ≥ 1000 = typically non-default, non-admin accounts (prime attack targets).
Multiple GPOs can be linked to one object; applied in link order.
BloodHound helps, but manual PowerView/Linux tool checks are required for complete coverage.
• displayname → Friendly name shown in GPMC.
• gpcfilesyspath → Path in SYSVOL containing GPO data for replication (e.g., \\domain\sysvol\domain\Policies\{GUID}).
• objectguid → Global unique ID for programmatic references to the GPO.
